title: The Trinity (CCC 253–256)
hook: one God in three persons, a communion of love

segments.voice: Yesterday: God is charity, God's very being is love. Your line was god is love. Did you manage your hidden kindness? Today, a puzzle hiding in that line. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

Here's a question a kid might ask at the dinner table. If God is love, who did God love before there was anything? Before the world, before angels, before people. Love needs someone to love, doesn't it? You can't really be love all by yourself in an empty room. It sounds like a riddle. For Catholics, the answer is the most central mystery of the faith, the one they name every time they make the sign of the cross. Today: the Trinity.
screen: `WHO DID GOD LOVE BEFORE ANYTHING?` → `LOVE NEEDS SOMEONE TO LOVE.` → `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Catholics believe in one God in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Jesus sends his apostles out, in the Douay-Rheims: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Notice: in the name, singular. One name, three persons. Second, what it doesn't mean. The Catechism, in paragraphs 253 to 256, is careful. It's not three gods. It's not one God wearing three masks, either. Each person is fully God, and the three are really distinct from one another, distinct only in how they relate: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds. Early councils, at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381, fought hard for that language, and nearly every Christian church still professes it in the Creed. Third, the answer to the riddle. If God is love, then from all eternity there is lover, beloved, and the love between them. Augustine put it almost that way sixteen centuries ago. God was never alone in an empty room. God is a communion, a life of self-giving love, before anything else existed. And creation, and each person, is invited into that love. Fourth, it's a mystery. The Catechism calls the Trinity the central mystery of Christian faith, something we couldn't have figured out, only received. There's a famous story that Saint Patrick used a three-leafed shamrock to explain it. It's a story people tell, not something in his own writings, and every picture falls short. The Church's honest answer is: this is who God is, and it's love all the way down.
screen: `ONE NAME, THREE PERSONS.` · `NOT THREE GODS, NOT THREE MASKS.` · `LOVER, BELOVED, AND LOVE.` · `THE CENTRAL MYSTERY.` · then, large: `LOVE IS A COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray, or hear, the Glory Be, slowly. It's one of the oldest and shortest Catholic prayers. Breathe between each phrase. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen. If you pray, say it once more on your own, slowly, then sit in the quiet after it. If you don't, just listen to its shape: three names, one glory, always. The bell holds the time.
The Trinity. One God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: the central mystery of Catholic faith, a communion of love. Today's word.
Your line: love is a communion. Today, notice a moment of real togetherness, a shared laugh, a meal, a hand held, and let it remind you what Catholics say God is. Day two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics begin and end prayer with the sign of the cross in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, pray the Glory Be after each decade of the rosary, and keep Trinity Sunday the week after Pentecost.

original.note: Latin: threeness, a word the early Latin writer Tertullian was among the first to use for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Trinity is a math problem, three equals one.
what it means: one God who is a communion of love, Father, Son and Spirit, from all eternity.
what a scholar hears: homoousios at Nicaea (325), the Spirit's divinity at Constantinople (381), Tertullian's trinitas, Augustine's lover-beloved-love, and CCC 253–256.

The Glory Be is a traditional prayer, given in the practice in its common modern American form ('Holy Spirit'); it is spoken, not presented as a quotation from a listed translation. Confirm wording used in the US.
'Nearly every Christian church still professes it in the Creed' — some groups (e.g. Oneness Pentecostals, Latter-day Saints, Jehovah's Witnesses) do not; confirm phrasing is acceptable.
Tertullian's early use of trinitas (c. 200) is standard; Theophilus of Antioch used the Greek trias earlier. Confirm the note's phrasing ('among the first').
The shamrock story is labeled a later story people tell.
